Pallid sturgeon Scaphirhynchus albus embryos, following fertilisation and development within a yolk-laden egg, undergo eclosion after a relatively brief incubation period. The age at eclosion, defined as the moment of chorion rupture leading to the emergence of the yolk-sac larva, has been recorded as 18.2 days [ab = 18.2 days] at a water temperature of 17.8 °C [T = 17.8 °C], a duration that aligns with the rapid early ontogeny observed in other Acipenseriform species under similar thermal regimes. Following this hatching event, the lecithotrophic larva remains entirely dependent on its endogenous yolk reserves for sustenance. The transition to exogenous feeding, which marks the beginning of independent nutritional intake and is considered the biological birth point for this species, occurs at 13 days post-hatch. At this critical stage of first feeding, the newly exotrophic individual possesses a wet body mass of only 0.0239 grams [Wwb = 0.0239 grams], a value reflecting the modest size of the prolarva at the onset of active prey capture in the turbid, fast-flowing waters of the Missouri River.

Estimates of longevity for this species are derived from field studies and mark-recapture data, with the maximum lifespan in the wild considered to be approximately 100 years [am = approximately 100 years] under the average thermal conditions of the Missouri River at 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. This remarkable longevity is characteristic of many large-bodied chondrostean fishes and is linked to their slow growth rates and delayed reproductive schedules. In contrast, the ultimate wet weight, representing the maximum recorded body mass sampled from wild populations and verified by angler catches, reaches 30,000 grams [Wwi = 30,000 grams]. This substantial mass is complemented by a corresponding fork length dimension; the largest pallid sturgeon reliably documented in both scientific sampling efforts and recreational angler records attained an ultimate fork length of 163.8 centimeters [Li = 163.8 centimeters], confirming the species' potential to achieve a truly massive body size over its century-long lifespan. The maximum reproduction rate reaches 233 eggs per day [Ri = 233 eggs per day] under optimal conditions at 13 °C [T = 13 °C].

Sexual maturation in pallid sturgeon proceeds at different rates between the sexes, a common pattern among iteroparous acipenserids. Under the prevailing thermal conditions of the lower Missouri River, estimated to average 13 °C [T = 13 °C] annually, female Scaphirhynchus albus typically attain puberty at approximately 15 years [tp = approximately 15 years]. This protracted period of somatic growth before gonadal recrudescence reflects the substantial energetic investment required for vitellogenesis in a large-bodied, late-maturing species. Conversely, male pallid sturgeon achieve puberty at a notably younger age, reaching this developmental state at approximately 12 years [tp = approximately 12 years] under the same temperature regime. at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]This sexual dimorphism in maturation timing is ecologically significant, as it ensures a pool of reproductively viable males is available to fertilize the eggs of the older, larger females during the infrequent spawning events that characterize this species' life history.

Reproductive output in pallid sturgeon is strongly correlated with female body size and is constrained by a biennial spawning periodicity. The most fecund females recorded in the literature produce an average of 170,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 170,000 eggs per spawning event], a fecundity value derived from the upper range of counts reported by field studies. However, because individual females do not spawn annually but exhibit a two-year interval between reproductive events, the effective annual frequency of reproduction is 0.5 spawnings per year [F_R_i = 0.5 spawnings per year]. Over a full calendar year, a maximally fecund female contributes the equivalent of 85,000 eggs per year [Ri = 85,000 eggs per year] to the population when accounting for the two-year spawning cycle. These reproductive parameters were observed at a mean Missouri River water temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], under which the energetic costs of gametogenesis and spawning migration are balanced against the available foraging resources.

Habitat degradation and river channelization have profoundly impacted the ecological niche of Scaphirhynchus albus, a species endemic to the Missouri and Mississippi River basins. The species requires extensive, unfragmented reaches of sandy, braided river channels with variable depth and turbidity for successful foraging and larval drift. Young larvae, after transitioning from their yolk-sac stage, must locate suitable invertebrate prey in the drift, a challenge compounded by altered flow regimes from dam operations. The species' slow growth and late maturity further exacerbate its vulnerability, as individuals must survive for approximately 15 years before reaching female puberty [tp = approximately 15 years before reaching female puberty] and contributing to the next generation at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. Furthermore, the documented maximum longevity of approximately 100 years [am = approximately 100 years] does not always translate into sustained recruitment; many older individuals exhibit signs of reproductive senescence or fail to encounter mates due to low population densities at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. Conservation efforts thus focus on restoring hydrographic variability and availability of spawning gravel bars to support the species' complex life cycle.
